1.he: ספרו המתואר מן החלומות דף תפ"ו
1.note: The page numbers refer to the sixteenth-century Latin edition of Philo that de' Rossi used; they are kept as given.

2.note: Marcus Tullius Cicero, Tusculan Disputations, Book I. The rabbinic saying is attributed to R. Meir in Bereshit Rabbah 9.

3.note: Philo, De fuga et inventione (On Flight and Finding).

4.note: Pimander, the first treatise of the Corpus Hermeticum, which Marsilio Ficino translated into Latin (1471).

5.he: ראש חכמי הנוצרים... קאמפירי"או איש ליא"וני
5.note: The 'chief of the Christian sages' is presumably Augustine. The Lyonnais scholar is Symphorien Champier, who commented on the Hermetic texts.

6.note: Sigismund Gelenius, whose Latin translation of Philo appeared in Lyon, 1555.

7.he: היוסיפון לרומיים ספר ד' פרק ח'
7.note: Josephus, Antiquities (cited by de' Rossi as 'Yosippon to the Romans'). The book and chapter numbering follow his edition and are kept as given.

8.note: Pseudo-Berossus and 'Metasthenes', texts from the forged collection of Annius of Viterbo, in which the pseudo-Philonic Breviarium de temporibus was also printed.

10.note: The cited chapter name and section numbers are kept as given; the Bereshit Rabbah reference for Dinah and Job is usually 57 rather than 19.

11.note: Agostino Steuco (Eugubinus), author of the Recognitio Veteris Testamenti.

12.note: The Mekhilta (Beshallah) counts four factions; Pseudo-Philo (LAB 10) has three. The number is kept as the author gives it.

13.note: The reference is unclear. The passage is in b. Sanhedrin 20b; 'כ"ג' may be a folio or chapter number in the author's edition.

14.note: The seven forms of rule are discussed in Plato's Statesman (Politicus); the designation 'sixteenth book' presumably reflects the ordering of the edition de' Rossi used.

15.note: Paul, Romans 13:9, which lists 'You shall not commit adultery' before 'You shall not kill'.

16.note: Presumably Jerome, the Latin translator of Eusebius's Chronicle.
